english: Let $S$ denote the set of all $3\times3$ matrices $A$ with integer entries such that $A$ is symmetric and $AA^{T}=I$, where $I$ is the $3\times3$ identity matrix. Then the number of elements of $S$ is ______.
hindi: माना कि $S$ पूर्णांक प्रविष्टियों वाले उन सभी $3\times3$ आव्यूहों $A$ का समुच्चय है जिनके लिए $A$ सममित है तथा $AA^{T}=I$ है, जहाँ $I$, $3\times3$ तत्समक आव्यूह है। तब $S$ के अवयवों की संख्या ______ है।
solution: $AA^{T}=I$: each row has $\sum a_{ij}^{2}=1$ with integer entries, so each row has one entry $\pm1$ and the rest $0$
Rows are also mutually orthogonal, so the $\pm1$'s are in different columns: $A$ is a permutation matrix with signs
Symmetric $\Rightarrow$ the permutation $\sigma$ satisfies $\sigma=\sigma^{-1}$, and $a_{ij}=a_{ji}$ for the paired places
$\sigma=$ a transposition $(i\ j)$ ($3$ choices): $a_{ij}=a_{ji}=\pm1$ ($2$ ways), fixed diagonal entry $\pm1$ ($2$ ways): $3\times4=12$
A $3$-cycle is not its own inverse, so total $=8+12=20$
solution_full: From $AA^{T}=I$, the $(i,i)$ entry gives $a_{i1}^{2}+a_{i2}^{2}+a_{i3}^{2}=1$. With integer entries, each row has exactly one entry equal to $\pm1$ and the other two equal to $0$.

The $(i,k)$ entry for $i\neq k$ gives that rows $i$ and $k$ are perpendicular; if their non-zero entries were in the same column the dot product would be $\pm1$. So the non-zero entries lie in different columns.
Hence $A$ is a signed permutation matrix: $a_{i\sigma(i)}=\varepsilon_i\in\{1,-1\}$ for a permutation $\sigma$ of $\{1,2,3\}$, all other entries $0$. Every such matrix satisfies $AA^{T}=I$.
Symmetry $a_{ij}=a_{ji}$: the non-zero pattern must be symmetric, so $\sigma(\sigma(i))=i$ for all $i$, i.e. $\sigma$ is the identity or a transposition; a $3$-cycle is excluded.

Transposition swapping $i,j$ and fixing $k$ (three choices of the pair): symmetry forces $a_{ij}=a_{ji}=\varepsilon\in\{\pm1\}$, and $a_{kk}=\pm1$, giving $2\times2=4$ matrices per pair, so $3\times4=12$.
For example $\begin{pmatrix}0&-1&0\\-1&0&0\\0&0&1\end{pmatrix}$ is in $S$, while $\begin{pmatrix}0&1&0\\-1&0&0\\0&0&1\end{pmatrix}$ is orthogonal but not symmetric.
originality_note: New: integer orthogonal matrices are signed permutation matrices, and the symmetric ones correspond to involutions with matching signs (way 5). Closest known: 2025-P1-Q4, counting integer orthogonal 3 x 3 matrices commuting with diag(2,2,3). Different because: the extra condition is symmetry, which turns the count into involutions of S_3 with sign constraints.

concept_use.Special types of square matrices: Symmetry a_ij = a_ji forces the underlying permutation to be its own inverse and the paired signs to agree, which cuts the 48 signed permutation matrices to 20.
concept_use.Orthogonal matrices: AA^T = I with integer entries forces unit rows that are pairwise perpendicular, i.e. signed permutation matrices.

stem_review: Read as a student: every matrix and symbol is defined before use, every condition is stated, each sentence has one reading; the answer was recomputed with sympy and is unique and equal to the Answer Plan; no hyperbolic functions or asymptotes. Checked: brute force over all symmetric matrices with entries in {-1,0,1} (integer orthogonal matrices cannot have other entries) gives exactly 20 with AA^T = I. Changed: No change.
key_step: Reducing integer orthogonal matrices to signed permutation matrices, then counting symmetric ones as involutions with equal paired signs.
justification: Two linked ideas (orthogonality with integer entries forces signed permutations; symmetry forces involutions) and a small count with no options. Same family as 2025-P1-Q4 (L4), but with a lighter final count, so one level below it.
